intended_object: This is the splitting isomorphism from the splitting lemma. If f : A → B is a linear map with a right inverse g (f ∘ g = id), then ker f × B ≅ A by (k, b) ↦ k + g(b), with inverse a ↦ (a − g(f a), f a). I took this from the docstring, which cites Weibel's K-book §I.1.2.1.
explanation:
The forward map is `ker.subtype.coprod g`, so it sends (k, b) to k + g b. The inverse is `(codRestrict (id − g∘f)).prod f`, so it sends a to (a − g(f a), f a). The membership proof is valid: f(a − g(f a)) = f a − f a = 0. The code checks this after applying g, which is fine because g is injective. Both round-trip identities are proved, and they are the standard computations.

The generality is right. A must be an additive group because the inverse uses subtraction. B only needs to be an additive monoid, and in fact it is automatically a group, since it is a retract of A. Only a semiring of scalars is needed.

Mathlib's `Function.Exact.splitSurjectiveEquiv` gives the same splitting in a different form. It starts from an exact sequence 0 → M → N → P and asks all three modules to be additive groups. So Mathlib is not more general here. This definition is a direct, fully explicit version stated in terms of `ker f`, and it matches the textbook construction.
